C0.quote: We consider voting on multiple independent binary issues.
C0.note: Aggregation of binary votes on several issues into one proposal (issue-wise majority, Condorcet winners).

C1.quote: it is co-NP-hard to determine whether there exists a Condorcet-winning proposal
C1.note: Complexity and recognition algorithms (Thms 1, 7, 8, 10). Domain conditions and paradox-free or existence results (Thms 4, 9, 11-14) coded AX.

C2.1.value: preference profile; vote v_i; weight profile
C2.1.quote: the opinion/preference 𝑣𝑖,𝑗 ∈ B of voter 𝑖 on issue 𝑗

C2.2.quote: The decision space for each issue is B := {±1}.
C2.2.note: Binary ±1 vectors over issues, plus weight vectors over issues (external or per-voter internal).

C2.3.quote: the opinion/preference 𝑣𝑖,𝑗 ∈ B of voter 𝑖 on issue 𝑗
C2.3.note: Opinions/preferences, and weights as perceived issue importance.

C2.4.quote: Each voter 𝑖 ∈ [𝑛] is modeled as a dimension-𝑡 vector
C2.4.note: The input is the preference itself. Weights are 'reported', but nothing is said about truthful reporting.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used for this model.

C5.1.note: Results evaluate majority support, Condorcet winning and distance to IWM. Voter satisfaction appears only as future work in the conclusion.

VOT.quote_behav: each voter votes for whichever of 𝑝 and 𝑝 ′ agrees with
VOT.note: Voters vote by weighted Hamming agreement.

ORG.note: A policymaker setting external weights is mentioned in the introduction, but the weights are exogenous in the model.

claims.quote: this would allow for practically certifying “safe instances” where issue-wise majority
in which returning an IWM proposal is always a good choice
we need not fear a vote being called against the defeating proposal

C9.2.note: Claims about real proposal choice need submitted opinions to equal voters' actual views, which is not stated. The 'need not fear' claim needs an unmodelled computationally bounded strategic opposer who calls votes.
